Question: What is the opposite of buoyancy?
Answer: Buoyancy doesn't really have an “opposite” force. Buoyancy is like heat and light. The “opposite” of buoyancy is just a lack of it, and there's no name for it. (Cold and shadow aren't really “things,” they are just a lack of heat and light with names.) The buoyant force pushes upward. If you have more buoyant force than your weight, you float. If you have less buoyant force than your weight, you sink. So the buoyant force acts against your weight due to gravity, and gravity is an opposing force. But gravity not really the “opposite” of buoyancy either though, it's the same thing. Gravity causes buoyancy to happen in the first place! Gravity pushes down on a fluid which creates a pressure gradient in the medium. This pressure supports the weight of objects within the medium in the form of buoyancy. If the object weighs more than the buoyant force, then gravity pulls the object down within the medium. If the buoyant force is greater than the weight, the object floats upward. So there's nothing like an “anti-buoyancy.” You either have enough buoyancy or you don't. If you sink, it's because you don't. But matter nearly always has some positive amount of buoyancy. The “opposite” of buoyancy is just a lack of sufficient buoyancy, and there's no name for it. OP: “What is the opposite of buoyancy?”

Question: Can you clarify the distinction between "predict" and "estimate" in the context of science? What is the reasoning behind this difference?
Answer: In scientific terms, a prediction is just what it sounds like, Quora robot. It is a forecast of the future based on a theory, which was in turn based on past observations. The predictive power of theories is how we can test them. We anticipate the outcome of a test or experiment, and then we perform the test or experiment to check the anticipated prediction. An estimate is simply the rounding off of a numerical value. It just means an “imprecise” numerical value. It is wildly different from a prediction in that an estimate in science has absolutely nothing to do with anticipating the future. Unlike the common usage, in science, an estimate only means a numerical value that is not exact, and does not have anything to do with anticipating a future outcome. So even though “an estimate” in common usage can mean something similar to a “prediction,” in science, an estimate has nothing to do with a prediction, unless it is a prediction of a numerical value. In that particular case, an estimate can be a part of the prediction. Otherwise, they are two different things. An estimate is not a prediction in science. Question: Why does a balloon filled with helium gas go up when it is not held?

The helium balloon literally floats on air just like a boat floats on water. This upward push is called the buoyant force. You can do the same thing with a ball in a pool. Get an inflated sports ball, like a soccerball or a volleyball. Push it down into the water of the pool. The ball will resist being submerged and buoyancy will fight really hard to get the ball back to the surface. This is because gravity is pushing down on the water, and that same pressure create a buoyant force that pushes the ball back up. The difference in density between the air in the ball and the surrounding water is much greater, so the buoyant force is much stronger. But the sports ball in the water and the helium balloon in the air are doing the same thing. They are both being pushed up by the buoyant force caused by the difference in the density surrounding medium, and the pressure gradient due to Earth's gravity.
